title: Everything We Know About Squids
summary: Josh and Chuck explore squid: their roughly 300 species split into two suborders (Myopsida and Oegopsida), notable species such as the California market squid, European squid, Caribbean reef squid, Humboldt squid, deep sea luminescent squid, and the vampire squid from hell, plus the long-armed ptychoteuthid deep-sea squid. They cover squid anatomy (pen internal shell, beak, radula, eight arms and two tentacles), intelligence (around 500 million neurons, comparable to a dog), chromatophore skin signaling, reproduction and egg guarding, squid ink (composition, uses in pasta, medicine, and defense, and jet propulsion), giant and colossal squid (2005 capture and filming in Japan, 2007 colossal squid catch near Antarctica), and the ethics of eating calamari. The episode closes with a listener email from David about handling a Mars meteorite and Buzz Aldrin's moon rock as a police evidence tech.

entities.name: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

segments.title: Opening and squid overview
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on squid, describe their weird appearance, and note that squid have been around at least 100 million years and that roughly 300 species fall into two suborders.

segments.title: Shallow-water squid species
segments.summary: They discuss the California market squid, the European squid, and the Caribbean reef squid, including their ranges, sizes, and fishing, and mention the cuttlefish as a close relative.

segments.title: Deep-sea squid species
segments.summary: They cover deep-dwelling squid including the short finned squid's migration, the deep sea luminescent squid with photophores, and the Humboldt squid, known as the red devil.

segments.title: Vampire squid from hell and the finned squid
segments.summary: They describe the vampire squid from hell, a living-fossil cephalopod that feeds on marine snow, and the finned squid with very long arms found in deep water in the Philippine Sea.

segments.title: Squid anatomy and classification
segments.summary: They discuss squid being mollusks with an internal pen instead of a shell, their place among cephalopods alongside octopus, cuttlefish, and nautilus, and how squid arms and tentacles differ.

segments.title: Origins and evolution of squid
segments.summary: They discuss when cephalopods and squid evolved, linking cephalopods to the Cambrian Explosion and squid divergence to the Mesozoic marine revolution, and the wide size range of squid.

segments.title: Squid beaks, intelligence, and chromatophores
segments.summary: They describe the parrot-like beak and radula, the squid's neuron count of about 500 million comparable to a dog, the different kind of alien intelligence, and chromatophore skin signaling used in mating displays.

segments.title: Squid reproduction
segments.summary: They describe squid mating, in which males transfer sperm packets to the female's mouth cavity, and the female guarding fertilized eggs before both parents die.

segments.title: Squid ink
segments.summary: They cover squid ink as food in pasta, its composition (melanin, mucus, amino acids, metals), its uses in medicine, its use as a defense and shape-casting cloud, and the jet propulsion that lets squid escape quickly.

segments.title: Giant and colossal squid
segments.summary: They recount sea monster lore, the first filmed giant squid in 2005 by Japanese researchers, the 2006 capture, and the 2007 colossal squid caught near Antarctica by a New Zealand ship.

segments.title: Eating squid and calamari
segments.summary: They discuss calamari as Italian for squid, the size of calamari from a colossal squid, the ethics of eating intelligent animals, and personal anecdotes about squid sushi.

segments.title: Listener mail: Mars rock and moon rock
segments.summary: Listener David describes working as a police evidence tech, storing a Mars rock and a moon rock from NASA overnight, including a moon rock handpicked by Buzz Aldrin.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and invite listeners to send their own stories by email.
